feed.title: Combined summary - A STARK proof of Bitcoin's UTXO set at block 972,500, with circuits proven in Lean

entry.title: Combined summary - A STARK proof of Bitcoin's UTXO set at block 972,500, with circuits proven in Lean
entry.summary: A novel side project applies a STARK-based cryptographic proof system to Bitcoin’s consensus, producing a single compact proof that can be efficiently verified in a web browser. The demonstration and source code are publicly available at [Starked Bitcoin Demo](https://starknet-innovation.github.io/starked-bitcoin/) and [GitHub Repository](https://github.com/starknet-innovation/starked-bitcoin), respectively. The project generates a 1.6 MB proof file—referred to as the “seal”—which verifies, with high confidence and transparency, three primary aspects: the integrity of block headers from genesis to the latest tip under Bitcoin Core’s rules (excluding only the wall-clock time-too-new check), complete replay and validation of blocks 935,001 through 972,500 matching raw data and structural rules, and confirmation of the resulting UTXO set identical to what Bitcoin Core would produce, including a Merkle root commitment for granular proofs. This design enables efficient SPV-style verification, supports independent validation, and allows for compact inclusion/exclusion proofs for specific outputs. Certain limitations are acknowledged in this proof architecture. Script verification and signature checks are excluded, aligning the trust model with Bitcoin Core’s assumevalid and assumeUTXO modes. Witness data is included to permit future addition of script validation modules without requiring a full recomputation of prior proofs. The replayed segment begins from Core’s assumeUTXO snapshot at block 935,000, with earlier blocks covered solely by their headers. Full end-to-end proof from genesis remains computationally intensive, estimated at about 325 H100 GPU-hours, which currently impedes practical implementation but remains a target for future iterations as efficiency improves. The approach leverages Stwo, a circle STARKs implementation over M31, accessible via a Zig port ([Stwo-Zig](https://github.com/teddyjfpender/stwo-zig)), utilizing a CUDA backend for performance and recursive aggregation. Circuits are specified in Lean 4, exported for proving, and rigorously machine-checked for correctness using differential fuzz testing against Bitcoin Core’s C++ logic. These tests have demonstrated behavioral equivalence across hundreds of thousands of cases, though they fall short of formal equivalence proofs. Trust assumptions extend to the soundness of underlying cryptographic primitives and Fiat–Shamir heuristics in the random oracle model, further detailed in [verification.md](https://github.com/starknet-innovation/starked-bitcoin/blob/a3e06f53f8b28310933265540e8b4189fe630f66/docs/reference/verification.md). A significant utility arising from this work is the verify-snapshot tool, enabling anyone to independently validate an assumeUTXO snapshot’s base block, coin count, total amount, and hash_serialized against the STARK proof. On standard hardware, this process has been shown to verify a 9.39 GB snapshot containing over 164 million coins in just seventy-two seconds, using minimal memory. Of this time, nearly all is consumed by reading and hashing the large snapshot; actual proof verification executes in under half a second, illustrating the potential for scalable, resource-efficient validation. Lean’s role in formalizing and verifying mathematical proofs opens new possibilities for cryptographic protocol innovation. While batch signature verification offers theoretical efficiency gains—especially via hardware acceleration platforms like [RiscZero](https://www.risczero.com)—practical constraints remain, particularly concerning secp256k1 operations within STARKs and transitioning from ECDSA to Schnorr signatures for batching opportunities. Verification complexity, currently O(log² n), is a recognized bottleneck, but techniques such as Risc Zero’s “shrink wrap” (using Groth16 proofs) could transfer most computational burden to proof generation, rendering real-time verification nearly trivial. This trade-off, however, necessitates giving up hash-only post-quantum security for smaller proof sizes, which may not always align with network priorities. The layered proof architecture mirrors robust best practices in blockchain validation. Header chains are validated via lightweight proof-of-work, median time, and version signaling—tasks well-suited for light clients and not requiring zero-knowledge proofs. Commitments to per-block undo data and incremental UTXO set updates reinforce block validation’s consistency and adaptability. Each block’s undo data ensures proper transaction ordering, coinbase handling, and exact consumption of UTXOs, while adhering to rules on coinbase subsidy, fees, script logic, timelocks, maturity, weight, and sigops limits. Focusing on UTXO set transitions, rather than per-block validation alone, offers improved resilience to soft forks and more flexible proof construction. This allows nodes to validate only new blocks atop widely trusted checkpoints or zkproof sets, reducing redundant computation and enhancing scalability.
